quote: "You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower." — Epictetus, Discourses, Book I, Chapter 1
context:
Epictetus was answering a question that must have come up constantly among his students: what can a tyrant actually take from you? He traces the list down to its end. The body can be chained, exiled, killed. But the faculty of choice, the part that assents or refuses, lies outside any jailer's reach. He is not offering comfort. He is drawing a boundary, insisting that the one thing worth guarding is the one thing no guard can touch.

That boundary was tested this week in a different cell. The Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich published a memoir of the nearly five hundred days he spent in Russian prisons after a false arrest for espionage. 
He was detained in March 2023 and released in August 2024
 in a multi-country prisoner swap. 
The book is described as a testament to the humanity he refused to surrender.
 The walls held his body. What he kept was the thing Epictetus marked off as his own.
question: When circumstances strip away everything you cannot control, do you know exactly what is left that still answers to you alone?
